# Shaping and the final proof

Shaping builds a taut skin on the outside of a loaf so it holds its form and expands upward in the oven instead of spreading flat. For a round boule the technique is to fold the edges into the center, flip the dough seam side down and drag it across the work surface so friction tightens the skin against the table. A batard gets the same folding followed by a gentle roll into an oval. The dough should feel taut but not torn — ripping the skin destroys the tension it was built to create.

After shaping comes the final proof, the second rise that rebuilds the gas network the shaping knocked down. The dough rises again until nearly but not quite doubled. The poke test judges readiness: press a floured finger half a centimeter in — if the dent springs back slowly and leaves a shallow mark, the loaf is ready; springing back instantly means underproofed, while a dent that stays deep or collapses means overproofed.

Final proofing runs warm and fast on the counter or cold and slow overnight in the refrigerator, the retarded proof, which also makes the loaf easier to score and deepens flavor. Proof boules seam side up in a floured basket so the tension stays where it matters. Rushing the proof gives dense bread that bursts unpredictably; letting it run too long gives a slack loaf that collapses at the oven door.
